Janet Ward Black (February 15, 1959 – November 2, 2025) was an American lawyer and legal leader in North Carolina. She founded and owned Ward Black Law, one of the state’s largest female-owned personal injury law firms. Black served as president of the North Carolina Association of Trial Lawyers (now North Carolina Advocates for Justice) and was the fourth woman to hold the presidency of the North Carolina Bar Association; she was the second lawyer in history to serve as president of both organizations. At the time of her death, she was serving as Vice-Chair of the Board of Legal Aid of North Carolina.
Earlier in her life, Black won the Miss Charlotte-Mecklenburg and Miss North Carolina pageants and competed in the Miss America pageant. She graduated cum laude from Davidson College in 1982 and earned her law degree from Duke University School of Law in 1985.
Throughout her career, Black promoted access to justice and public service. She founded pro bono initiatives, including the 4ALL program, and implemented charitable giving through her firm, reflecting her commitment to community support. She was recognized with several awards, including the Order of the Long Leaf Pine and induction into the North Carolina Bar Association Legal Practice Hall of Fame.
Early life and education
Janet Ward Black was born on February 15, 1959, in Kannapolis, North Carolina. Her father owned a small chain of pharmacies, and her mother taught English at Concord High School.
Black initially aspired to become a physician and attended Davidson College on a chemistry scholarship before deciding to pursue law. She was the first woman from Cabarrus County admitted to Davidson College.
During her third year at Davidson, Black won the Miss Charlotte-Mecklenburg pageant. In 1980, she won the Miss North Carolina pageant and took a leave of absence to serve as Miss North Carolina 1980. She later competed in the Miss America pageant, receiving a grand talent award for her piano performance of Chopin’s Revolutionary Étude.
She returned to Davidson College and graduated cum laude in 1982 with a degree in economics, then earned her Juris Doctor from Duke University School of Law in 1985.
Career
After initially practicing corporate law, Black became an assistant district attorney serving Cabarrus and Rowan counties from 1985 to 1988, becoming the first woman to hold the position in those jurisdictions.
From 1989 to 1992, she practiced litigation at Wallace Whitley Pope & Black in Salisbury, North Carolina, and later joined Donaldson & Black in Greensboro, where she worked until 2006.
In 2006, Black founded Ward Black Law in Greensboro, North Carolina. Under her leadership, the firm grew into a prominent woman-owned personal injury practice handling motor vehicle, workers’ compensation, and product liability cases.
The firm received national recognition from U.S. News & World Report, and Black was named Personal Injury “Lawyer of the Year” in the Triad region on two occasions.
Black also held leadership roles within professional legal organizations and served on advisory boards supporting legal education and advocacy.
Black served as president of the North Carolina Bar Association and Foundation from 2007 to 2008. During her tenure, she founded the 4ALL program, a statewide telephone legal advice initiative that later served as a model for similar programs nationwide and in Canada. The program has provided free legal assistance to tens of thousands of North Carolinians.  Under her leadership, the NCBA expanded fundraising for Legal Aid of North Carolina’s Loan Repayment Assistance Program, raising over $860,000 toward its goal of supporting legal aid attorneys with law school loan repayment.
In October 2025, Black was inducted into the North Carolina Bar Association Legal Practice Hall of Fame.
Public service and legacy
Black’s work extended beyond her legal practice to include sustained involvement in community service, charitable initiatives, and professional mentorship. Influenced by her Christian faith, she implemented a policy at Ward Black Law to donate ten percent of the firm’s gross revenue to charitable organizations, a practice she publicly described as relying on “God’s math.”
Under her leadership, Ward Black Law also supported international mission trips and a range of local and regional nonprofit organizations, and encouraged firm-wide participation in community service initiatives.
Black was also active in mentorship and outreach efforts, particularly encouraging young women to pursue careers in law. She frequently spoke to students and community groups, including programs aimed at supporting female students and young professionals considering legal careers. Each year since 1989, Black was a keynote speaker at the American Legion Auxiliary Tar Heel Girls State. Several profiles noted that she emphasized the importance of increasing opportunities for women in the legal profession, drawing on her experiences entering a field in which relatively few women held leadership roles at the time.
In recognition of her civic and professional contributions, Black received the Long Leaf Pine Award, one of North Carolina’s highest civilian honors.
Awards and honors
* Miss North Carolina, 1980
* Order of the Long Leaf Pine
* Legal Practice Hall of Fame, North Carolina Bar Association, 2025
* Distinguished Service Award, North Carolina State Bar
* Advocate’s Award, NCBA Litigation Section
* Top Elon Law Award, Elon University School of Law
Personal life and death
Black met her husband, Gerard Davidson, while they were on opposite sides of a lawsuit, and they later married in 1995. Davidson joined Ward Black Law in 2013. Black had two stepsons, Clay and Walker Davidson; her oldest stepson also worked at Ward Black Law. The couple owned a German Shepherd.
In May 2025, Black was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). She died on November 2, 2025, at the age of 66. A memorial service was held on November 14, 2025, at First Presbyterian Church in Greensboro and was attended by hundreds of people.
